items.prompt: State what is meant by the term oxbow lake.
items.canonical_answer: A horseshoe-shaped lake left beside a river when a meander bend is cut off.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - a lake formed from a cut-off meander bend. "A lake by a river" alone is not enough.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 structural exemplar from the topic 2.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain why a river cliff forms on the outside of a meander bend.
items.canonical_answer: The water flows fastest on the outside of the bend, so it has the most energy there. That energy erodes the outer bank by hydraulic action and abrasion. Because the bank is worn away underneath, it becomes a steep river cliff.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: fastest flow on the outside; which causes erosion of the bank (a named process); so the bank is undercut into a steep cliff.
An answer about deposition explains the inner bank, not the cliff.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 structural exemplar from the topic 2.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt:
Students measured the depth of a river across a meander bend, from the inner bank (0 m) to the outer bank (6 m):

| distance from inner bank / m | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| depth / m | 0.0 | 0.1 | 0.3 | 0.5 | 0.8 | 1.1 | 1.3 |

Describe how the depth changes across the bend.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows the river getting deeper from the inner bank to the outer bank. It is only 0.1 m deep 1 m from the inner bank, but 1.3 m deep at the outer bank. The depth rises steadily across the channel, and fastest near the outer bank.
marking_guidance: Reading: the overall pattern read from the table - deeper towards the outer bank (1 mark).
Figures: the shallowest and deepest values with their units, so the figures support the words (1 mark); the steeper change near the outer bank (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 structural exemplar from the topic 2.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner describes the channels that split away from a river near its mouth as "tributaries". Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: Tributaries join a river and add water to it. Channels that split away from a river near the sea are distributaries, which carry water away from the main river.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the confusion named - tributary and distributary are not the same (joining a river, not leaving it).
1 mark: the correct term, distributary, and where it is found (a delta).

items.prompt: For the River Nile in Egypt, describe two opportunities the Aswan High Dam provides.
items.canonical_answer: Lake Nasser stores water behind the dam, so farms downstream can be irrigated all year and grow more than one crop a year. The dam also generates hydro-electric power for Egypt’s towns and industry.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per developed point, 2 in all: stored water for all-year irrigation; hydro-electric power.
Each fact is a feature of the named example, not a general point about dams.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 structural exemplar from the topic 2.2 claim ledger.

items.prompt: For a named river you have studied, explain how people have managed the hazards of the river, and describe the problems the management has caused. [7]
items.canonical_answer:
The River Nile in Egypt used to flood its valley every year. The Aswan High Dam, completed in 1970 in southern Egypt, now controls that flood: the water is held back in Lake Nasser and released steadily, so the valley no longer floods and farms and towns are protected. The stored water also means farmers can irrigate all year and grow more than one crop a year, and the dam generates hydro-electric power.

The management has caused problems. The silt the flood once spread over the fields is now trapped in Lake Nasser, so farmers have to buy artificial fertiliser, which costs them money and can pollute the water. With less sediment reaching the sea, parts of the Nile delta coast are being eroded. Building the dam and the lake also meant that people living in the flooded area had to be moved.
marking_guidance: Level 1 (1-3): simple statements about managing a river, with no named example or only general points about dams.
Level 2 (4-6): developed and linked statements about a named river; capped at 5 if no named example is given.
Level 3 (7): comprehensive statements with place-specific detail - the Aswan High Dam, Lake Nasser, the delta, the date - covering both the management and its problems.

items.prompt:
This describes a stretch of a river seen from the air: a wide, flat valley floor; the river curves in five large bends; on the outside of each bend there is a steep bank about 2 m high; on the inside there are banks of sand; a curved lake lies 300 m from the river, next to a straight stretch of channel.
(a) Identify the landform formed by the curved lake. [1]
(b) Describe the evidence that the river erodes the outside of its bends. [2]
(c) Suggest how the curved lake was formed. [3]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) An oxbow lake.
(b) The steep 2 m banks on the outside of each bend show where the river has worn the bank away, and the sand banks on the inside show that the river drops its load there instead.
(c) The lake was probably once a meander bend. Erosion of the outer banks narrowed the neck between two bends until a flood cut through it, and the river took the straight course. Deposition then sealed the ends of the old bend, leaving the curved lake.
marking_guidance: Resource: (a) 1 mark for the landform named from the description.
Evidence: (b) 2 marks - the steep outer banks, then the contrast with the sand on the inside; each point uses the resource.
Figures and reasons: (c) 3 marks for the sequence - erosion narrows the neck, a flood cuts through, deposition seals the bend.
